questions.q: The angle between the lines whose direction cosines are given by the equations $3 l+m+5 n=0,6 \mathrm{ nm}-2 \mathrm{n} l+5 l \mathrm{m}=0$ is
questions.solution:
The given equations are
$3 l+m+5 n=0$...(i)
and $6 \mathrm{mn}-2 \mathrm{n} l+5 l \mathrm{m}=0$...(ii)
From (i), we have $m=-3 l-5 n$.
Putting $\mathrm{m}=-3 l-5 \mathrm{n}$ in (ii),
we get $6(-3 l-5 n) n-2 n l+5 l(-3 l-5 n)=0\Rightarrow(n+l)(2 n+l)=0\Rightarrow$ either $l=-\mathrm{n}$ or $l=-2 \mathrm{n}$.
If $l=-n$, then putting $l=-n$ in (i), we obtain $m=-2 n$.
If $l=-2 \mathrm{n}$, then putting $l=-2 \mathrm{n}$ in (i), we obtain $\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{n}$.
Thus, the direction ratios of two lines are $-\mathrm{n},-2 \mathrm{n}, \mathrm{n} and -2 \mathrm{n}, \mathrm{n}, \mathrm{n}$ i.e., $1,2,-1 and -2,1,1$.
Hence, the direction cosines are
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}, \frac{-1}{\sqrt{6}}$ or $\frac{-2}{\sqrt{6}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$. The angle $\theta$
between the lines is given by
$\begin{aligned}
& \cos \theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \times \frac{-2}{\sqrt{6}}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}+\frac{-1}{\sqrt{6}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}=\frac{-1}{6} \\
& \Rightarrow \theta=\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{-1}{6}\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Two planes are coplanar if
$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}x_2-x_1 & y_2-y_1 & z_2-z_1 \\ l_1 & m_1 & n_1 \\ l_2 & m_2 & n_2\end{array}\right|=0$
$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -k \\ k & 2 & 1\end{array}\right|=0$
Applying $\mathrm{C}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_2+\mathrm{C}_1, \mathrm{C}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_3+\mathrm{C}_1$
$\Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1-k \\ k & k+2 & 1+k\end{array}\right|=0$
$\Rightarrow \quad 1[2+2 k-(k+2)(1-k)]=0$
$\Rightarrow \quad 2+2 k-\left(-k^2-k+2\right)=0$
$k^2+3 k=0 \Rightarrow k(k+3)=0$

questions.q: Reflection of the line $\dfrac{x - 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{y - 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 4}{1}$ in the plane $x + y + z = 7$ is
questions.solution:
Given line $\dfrac{x - 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{y - 2}{3} = \dfrac{z - 4}{1}$ is passes through $P ( 1, 2, 4 )$.

To find the reflection of line we need one more point on the line clearly $M ( 0, 5, 5 )$ also lie on line.

Let $N ( \alpha, \beta, \gamma )$ be the reflection $M$ in the $x + y + z = 7$

$∴ \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + \dfrac{\beta + 5}{2} + \dfrac{\gamma + 5}{2} = 7$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = 4$

Also, $MN$ is perpendicular, i.e. parallel to the normal of the plane

$∴ \dfrac{\alpha}{1} = \dfrac{\beta - 5}{1} = \dfrac{\gamma - 5}{1} = \lambda$

$⇒ \alpha = \lambda, \beta = \lambda + 5, \gamma = \lambda + 5$

$∴ \lambda + \lambda + 5 + \lambda + 5 = 4$

$⇒ \lambda = - 2$

$∴ N = ( - 2, 3, 5 )$

Equation $PN$ is $\dfrac{x - 1}{- 3} = \dfrac{y - 2}{1} = \dfrac{z - 4}{- 1}$

questions.q: A line makes angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with the coordinate axes. If $\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{π}{2}$,~then $\left(cos\alpha + cos\beta + cos\gamma\right)2$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have, $\cos^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\beta + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$

$⇒ \cos^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$ [given $\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$]

$⇒ \cos^{2}\alpha + \sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$

$⇒ 1 + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$

$⇒ \cos^{2}\gamma = 0$

$⇒ cos\gamma = 0$

$∴ \left(cos\alpha + cos\beta + cos\gamma\right)^{2} = \left(cos\alpha + sin\alpha\right)^{2}$

$= 1 + 2sin\alpha \cdot cos\alpha = 1 + sin2\alpha$

$⇒ \$left($\dfrac{x + y + z}{3}\right)2 + \$ left($\dfrac{x - z}{2}\right)2 + \$ left($\dfrac{x - 2y + z}{6}\right)2 = p^{2}$

$⇒ 2\left(x + y + z\right)^{2} + 3\left(x - z\right)^{2} + \left(x - 2y + z\right)^{2} = 6p^{2}$

$⇒ 2x^{2} + 2y^{2} + 2z^{2} + 4xy + 4yz + 4zx + 3x^{2} + 3z^{2} - 6xz + x^{2} + 4y^{2} + z^{2} - 4xy - 4yz + 2xz = 6p^{2}$

$⇒ 6x^{2} + 6y + 6z^{2} = 6p^{2}$

$⇒ x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = p^{2}$

Hence, option (d) is correct.

questions.q: If the planes $\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \lambda\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) = 0$ and $\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(\lambda\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) = 5$ are perpendicular to each other, then the value of ${λ}^{2} + \lambda$ is
questions.solution:
We have,

$\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(\lambda\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) = 5$

$\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \lambda\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) = 0$

We know that two planes~$\overset{→}{r} \cdot \overset{→}{n}1 = {d}_{1}$~and& $\overset{→}{r} \cdot \overset{→}{n}2 = {d}_{2}$~are perpendicular if

$\overset{→}{n}1 \cdot \overset{→}{n}2 = 0$

Therefore,

$\left(\lambda\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \lambda\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) = 0$

$⇒ 2\lambda - 5\lambda - 3 = 0$

$⇒ - 3\lambda - 3 = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = - 1$

Therefore,~${λ}^{2} + \lambda = 0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $4  \left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}\right) and \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k},$ then \l$\left(sin\theta ++cos\theta\right)equals to$
questions.solution:
Let&

$\overset{→}{a} = \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{→}{b} = 4 \left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}\right)

Then,

\left|\overset{→}{a}\right| = \sqrt{{1}^{2} + {1}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = \sqrt{3}

\left|\overset{→}{b}\right| = \sqrt{{4}^{2} + {0}^{2} + \left(- 4\right)^{2}} =4\sqrt{2}

Now,

$ cos$\theta = \dfrac{\overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{b}}{\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|}

$⇒ cos$\theta = \dfrac{\left(\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(4\overset{^}{i} - 4\overset{^}{k}\right)}{\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|}

$⇒ cos$\theta = \dfrac{4 - 4}{\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|} =0$

Hence, $sin$\theta = $\sqrt{1 - \cos^{2}\theta} =1$

Therefore, $sin$\theta +$ cos$\theta =$1$

questions.q: The length of perpendicular drawn from the point $( 2, 3, 4 )$ to line $\dfrac{4 - x}{2} = \dfrac{y}{6} = \dfrac{1 - z}{3}$, is
questions.solution:
Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from $A ( 2, 3, 4 )$ to the given line $l$.

Then, $\dfrac{x - 4}{- 2} = \dfrac{y}{6} = \dfrac{z - 1}{- 3}$

Now, any point on the line $l$ is given by

$x = 4 - 2\lambda, y = 6\lambda, z = 1 - 3\lambda$

The coordinates of $P$ are $( 4 - 2\lambda, 6\lambda, 1 - 3\lambda )$

The direction ratios of $AP$ are

$( 4 - 2\lambda - 2, 6\lambda - 3, 1 - 3\lambda - 4 )$

i.e. $( 2 - 2\lambda, 6\lambda - 3, - 3 - 3\lambda )$

And the direction ratios of $l$ are$- 2, 6$ and $- 3$.

Given, $AP ⊥ l$

$∴ - 2 ( 2 - 2\lambda ) + 6 ( 6\lambda - 3 ) - 3 ( - 3 - 3\lambda ) = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{13}{49}$

$∴ AP^{2} = ( 4 - 2\lambda - 2{)}^{2} + ( 6\lambda - 3{)}^{2} + ( 1 - 3\lambda - 4{)}^{2}$

$= 22 - 26\lambda + 49{λ}^{2}$

Put $\lambda = \dfrac{13}{49}$, we get

$AP^{2} = \dfrac{909}{49} ⇒ AP = \dfrac{3}{7}\sqrt{101}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The image of the point $( 1, 6, 3 )$ in the line $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{3}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $P ( 1, 6, 3 )$ be the given point and $L$ be the foot of perpendicular from $P$ to the given line. The coordinates of a general point on the given line are

$\dfrac{x - 0}{1} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{3} = \lambda$ & (say)

i.e. $x = \lambda$

$y = 2\lambda + 1, z = 3\lambda + 2$

If the coordinates of $L$ are $( \lambda, 2\lambda + 1, 3\lambda + 2 )$, then the direction ratios of $PL$ are $( \lambda - 1, 2\lambda - 5, 3\lambda - 1 )$.

Since, the direction ratios of given line which is perpendicular to $PL$, are $1, 2$ and $3$. Therefore, $( \lambda - 1 ) 1 + ( 2\lambda - 5 ) 2 + ( 3\lambda - 1 )^{3} = 0$,which gives $\lambda = 1$.

Hence, coordinates of $L$ are $( 1, 3, 5 )$.

Let $Q \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}, {z}_{1}\right) be the image of $P ( 1, 6, 3 )$ in the given line. Then, $L$ is the mid-point of $PQ$.

Therefore, \dfrac{{x}_{1} + 1}{2} =1, \dfrac{{y}_{1} + 6}{2} =3, \dfrac{{z}_{1} + 3}{2} =5$

$⇒ {x}_{1} = 1, y = 0, z = 7$

Hence, the image of $( 1, 6, 3 )$ in the given line is $( 1, 0, 7 )$.

So, the equation of line $PQ$ is

$\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 5}{1} = \dfrac{z - 9}{1} = \lambda$

$⇒ x = \lambda + 1, y = \lambda - 5, z = \lambda + 9$

lies on the plane $x + y + z = 5$

$∴ ( \lambda + 1 ) - ( - \lambda + 5 ) + ( \lambda + 9 ) = 5$

$⇒ \lambda = - 10$

The coordinate of $Q$ is $( - 9, - 15, - 1 )$ and the coordinate of $P$ is $( 1, - 5, 9 )$

$PQ = \sqrt{( 10{)}^{2} + ( 10{)}^{2} + ( 10{)}^{2}} = 10\sqrt{3}$

$∴ 2\sqrt{3}k = 10\sqrt{3} ⇒ k = 5$

questions.q: Two lines $L_{1}: x=5, \frac{y}{3-\alpha}=\frac{z}{-2}\mathrm{L}_{2}: \mathrm{x}=\alpha, \frac{\mathrm{y}}{-1}=\frac{\mathrm{z}}{2-\alpha}$ are coplanar. Then, $\alpha \mathrm{can}$ take value (s)
questions.solution: The equations of given lines can be written as $\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{L}_{1}: \mathrm{x}-5=\frac{\mathrm{y}}{3-\alpha}=\frac{\mathrm{z}}{-2}\\ \mathrm{ L}_{2}: \mathrm{x}-\alpha=\frac{\mathrm{y}}{-1}=\frac{\mathrm{z}}{2-\alpha} \end{array}$ Since, these lines are coplanar. $\begin{array}{l}\text{ Therefore, }\left|\begin{array}{ccc}5-\alpha& 0-0 & 0-0 \\ 0 & 3-\alpha& -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2-\alpha \end{array}\right|$=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(5-\alpha)(3-\alpha)(2-\alpha)-2=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(5-\alpha) $\left(6-3 \alpha-2 \alpha+\alpha^{2}-2\right]$=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(5-\alpha) $\left(\alpha^{2}-5 \alpha+4\right]$=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad(5-\alpha)(\alpha-1)(\alpha-4)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \alpha=1,4,5 \end{array}

questions.q: A line makes the same angle $\theta$ with each of the $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Z}$ -axes. If the angle $\beta$, which it makes with Y-axis, is such that $\sin ^{2} \beta=3 \sin ^{2} \theta,$ then $\cos ^{2} \theta$ equals
questions.solution:
Let $l, \mathrm{~m}$ and $\mathrm{n}$ be the direction cosines. Then, $l=\cos \theta, \mathrm{m}=\cos \beta, \mathrm{n}=\cos \theta$

$\begin{array}{l}$$\text{ we have }$l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1 \\

\Rightarrow \cos ^{2} $\theta+\cos ^{2} \beta+\cos ^{2} \theta=$1 \\

\Rightarrow 2 \cos ^{2} $\theta+$1-\sin ^{2} $\beta=$1 \\

\Rightarrow 2 \cos ^{2} $\theta-\sin ^{2} \beta=$0 \\

\Rightarrow 2 \cos ^{2} $\theta-$3 \sin ^{2} $\beta=$0 \\

\quad$\left[\because \sin ^{2} \beta=$3 \sin ^{2} 0($\text{ given })\right]$\\

\Rightarrow \tan ^{2} $\theta=$2 / 3 \\

\therefore \cos ^{2} $\theta=\frac{1}{1+\tan ^{2} \theta}=\frac{1}{1+2 / 3}=\frac{3}{5}

\end{array}$

questions.solution:
If the given points be $A(2,3,4)$ and $B(6,7,8),$ then their mid-point $\mathrm{N}(4,5,6)$ must lie on the plane. The direction ratios of $\mathrm{AB}$ are $4,4,4,$ i.e. 1,1,1

questions.q: What is the value of $n$ so that the angle between the lines having direction ratios (1,1,1) and $(1,-1, n)$ is $60^{{}^{\circ}} ?$
questions.solution:
If $\left(l_{1}, m_{1}, n_{1}\right)$ and $\left(l_{2}, m_{2}, n_{2}\right)$ are the direction ratios then angle between the lines is
$\cos \theta=\frac{l_{1} l_{2}+m_{1} m_{2}+n_{1} n_{2}}{\sqrt{l_{1}^{2}+m_{1}^{2}+n_{1}^{2}} \sqrt{l_{2}^{2}+m_{2}^{2}+n_{2}^{2}}}$
Here l_{1}=1, m_{1}=1, n_{1}=1 and $l_{2}=1, m_{2}=-1, n_{2}=n and \theta=60^{{}^{\circ}}\therefore \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}}=\frac{1 \times 1+1 \times(-1)+1 \times n}{\sqrt{h^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2} \times} \sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}+y^{2}}}\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3} \sqrt{2+n^{2}}} \Rightarrow 3\left(2+n^{2}\right)=4 n^{2}\Rightarrow n^{2}=6 \Rightarrow n=\pm \sqrt{6}$

questions.q: The foot of the perpendicular from the point (7,14,5) to the plane $2 \mathrm{x}+4 \mathrm{y}-\mathrm{z}=2$ are
questions.solution:
We know that the length of the perpendicular from the point $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}\right)$ to the plane $a x+b y+c z+d=0$ is $\frac{\left|a x_{1}+b y_{1}+c z_{1}+d\right|}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}$
and the co-ordinate $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ of the foot of the $\perp$ are given by $\frac{\alpha-x_{1}}{a}=\frac{\beta-y_{1}}{b}=\frac{\gamma-z_{1}}{c}=- \left(\frac{a x_{1}+b y_{1}+c z_{1}+d}{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}\right) ...(1)$ In the given ques, x_{1}=7, y_{1}=14, z_{1}=5$,
$a=2 b=4, c=-1, d=-2By putting these values in $(1), we get \frac{\alpha-7}{2}=\frac{\beta-14}{4}=\frac{\gamma-5}{-1}=-\frac{63}{21}\Rightarrow \alpha=1, \beta=2 and $\gamma=$8$
Hence, foot of $\perp$ is (1,2,8)

questions.q: Find the coordinates of the point where the line joining the points (2,-3,1) and (3,-4,-5) cuts the plane $2 x+y+z=7$
questions.solution: The direction ratios of the line are $3-2,-4-(-3),-5-1$ i.e. 1,-1,-6 Hence equation of the line joining the given points is $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y+3}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{-6}=r($ say $)$ Coordinates of any point on this line are $(r+2,-r-3,-6 r+1)$ If this point lies on the given plane $2 x+y+z=7$ then $2(r+2)+(-r-3)+(-6 r+1)=7 \Rightarrow r=-1$ Coordinates of any point on this line are $(-1+2,-(-1)-3,-6(-1)+1)$ i.e. (1,-2,7)

questions.solution:
Since \(3(1)+2(-2)+(-1)(-1)=3-4+1=0\)
\(\therefore\) Given line is \(\perp\) to the normal to the plane i.e., given line is parallel to the given plane.
Also, \((1,-1,3)\) lies on the plane \(x-2 y-z=0\) if \(1-2(-1)-3=0\) i.e., \(1+2-3=0\) which is true \(\therefore\) L lies in plane \(\pi\).

questions.q: If the middle points of sides \(\mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CA} ~\&~ \mathrm{AB}\) of triangle \(A B C\) are respectively \(D, E, F\) then position vector of centre of triangle \(\mathrm{DEF}\), when position vector of \(A, B, C\) are respectively \(\hat{i}+\hat{j}\), \(\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \hat{\mathrm{k}}+\hat{\mathrm{i}}\) is -
questions.solution:
The position vector of points \(D, E, F\) are respectively
\(\frac{\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{j}}{2}+\mathrm{k}, \mathrm{i}+\frac{\mathrm{k}+\mathrm{j}}{2} \text{ and } \frac{\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{k}}{2}+\mathrm{j}\)
So, position vector of centre of \(\triangle \mathrm{DEF}\)
\(=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{j}}{2}+\mathrm{k}+\mathrm{i} \frac{\mathrm{k}+\mathrm{j}}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{k}}{2}+\mathrm{j}\right]=\frac{2}{3}[\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{j}+\mathrm{k}]\)

questions.q: The perpendicular distance of \(P(1,2,3)\) from the line \($\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-7}{2}=\frac{z-7}{-2}$\) is
questions.solution:
The point $\mathrm{A}(6,7,7)\) is on$ the $line. Let the perpendicular from \(\mathrm{P}\) meet the line in \(\mathrm{L}\). Then
\(\mathrm{AP}^2=(6-1)^2+(7-2)^2+(7-3)^2=66\)
Also \(\mathrm{AL}=\) projection of AP on line

\begin{aligned}& \left(\text{actual d.c.'s } \frac{3}{\sqrt{17}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}, \frac{-2}{\sqrt{17}}\right)\\
\Rightarrow & (6-1) \cdot \frac{3}{\sqrt{17}}+(7-2) \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}+(7-3) \frac{-2}{\sqrt{17}}\\
& =\sqrt{17}
\end{aligned}$
\(\therefore \perp\) distance \(\mathrm{d}\) of \(\mathrm{P}\) from the line is given by
\(\mathrm{d}^2=\mathrm{AP}^2-\mathrm{AL}^2=66-17=49 \text{ so that } \mathrm{d}=7\)
